title: E²-TTT: Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training
hook: Test-time training updates weights while it reads, but chunking for speed throws away the update's temporal structure. A closed-form state transition gets both.
key_points: Test-Time Training (TTT) handles long context by continuously updating fast weights during inference, one step per token.
Per-token updates are expressive but slow; chunk-wise approximations are hardware-friendly but discard the within-chunk update ordering.
E²-TTT derives a closed-form state transition that exactly reproduces the per-token recurrence's chunk-end fast-weight and momentum states.
That closed form allows fully parallel chunk-level training while preserving temporal structure — matching chunk-wise throughput.
Trained from scratch up to 1.3B params: on par in language modeling, better at in-context retrieval.
Biggest win is length extrapolation — over 90% Needle-in-a-Haystack passkey accuracy at 8x the training context.
content_html: Test-Time Training treats inference as a tiny training loop: as the model reads a long input, it keeps updating a set of "fast weights" so the sequence itself becomes the learning signal. Done strictly per token, that update rule is expressive but hopeless on GPUs; done in chunks, it parallelizes but flattens the ordering inside each chunk. Zeyun Zhong and colleagues propose E²-TTT, which under the standard approximation of taking gradients at chunk-start weights derives a closed-form state transition that exactly reproduces what the per-token recurrence would have produced at the chunk's end — fast weights and momentum both.
extra_html: Training models up to 1.3B parameters from scratch, the authors report parity with prior TTT and hybrid-attention baselines on language modeling, better in-context retrieval, and throughput matching the efficient chunk-wise methods. The headline result is length extrapolation: over 90% accuracy on the Needle-in-a-Haystack passkey test at eight times the training context length. Code is linked from the arXiv page.

related.title: Agentic Test-Time Training: Adapting Mid-Episode
related.hook: LLM agents degrade over long episodes, repeating failed moves — this method updates the model's weights continuously during the episode itself, but only on genuinely new information.

related.title: Feature Learning in Gated Delta Networks at Scale
related.hook: muP lets you tune hyperparameters on a small model and transfer them to a huge one. This paper derives the equivalent rules for gated delta networks, so sub-quadratic models scale without re-tuning.

related.title: Subquadratic Architectures: xLSTM vs. Mamba-2 vs. Gated DeltaNet
related.hook: Transformers pay a quadratic tax on sequence length. Pitting xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet head-to-head on hard tasks, xLSTM comes out ahead — and the paper explains why.

prereqs.title: What Are State-Space Models?
prereqs.hook: A compact hidden state summarizes everything seen so far - update it with each new input and you get sequence modeling that scales linearly, not quadratically.

flashcards.prompt: What trade-off do existing Test-Time Training methods face?
flashcards.back_html: Per-token weight updates are expressive but hardware-inefficient; chunk-wise approximations run fast but discard the temporal structure of the update rule within each chunk.

flashcards.prompt: What is E²-TTT's core technical move?

choices.text: A closed-form state transition that exactly reproduces the per-token recurrence's chunk-end fast-weight and momentum states
Dropping momentum so chunk updates commute
Shrinking the chunk size until it approaches per-token updates

flashcards.explanation_html: Under the standard chunk-start-gradient approximation, the authors derive an exact closed form for the chunk-end states — so chunks can be processed in parallel without losing the update rule's temporal structure.

flashcards.prompt: Where does E²-TTT's advantage show up most strongly?
flashcards.back_html: Length extrapolation: it keeps over 90% accuracy on the Needle-in-a-Haystack passkey test at 8x the context length it was trained on.
